en: The Jātaka,
Great Section, Chapter on the Mūgapakkha (The Dumb and Paralysed)
5. The Umāṅga Jātaka:
“Brahmadatta has arrived here with his entire army;”
In the evening, O Mahosadha, there was an immeasurable army of Pañcāla,
consisting of chariots and infantry.
Skilled in every battle,
she carries away [the enemy], sounding with a voice that awakens like the beating of kettledrums and conchs.
Adorned with the arts of metalwork,
possessing banners and mounts,
and well-provided with craftsmen.
They are well-established among the wise. Among them,
ten are said to be the wise ones—
those of vast wisdom who dwell in solitude.
Mātā Ekādasī rules over Pañcālī for the king;
then there are one hundred khattiyas here.
The illustrious followers,
their kingdom severed and trembling with fear,
have come under the power of Pañcāliya.
As long as the king’s executioners,
though acting against their will,
speak kindly, they follow after Pañcāla.
The inhabitants of Mithilā, though unwilling, were led away by that army which surrounded the city on three sides.
The capital of the Videhas is being besieged on all sides;
it is like a cluster of stars in the sky above.
They have surrounded him on all sides; O Mahosadha,
find out how his release may come to pass.
“Stretch out your feet, O King;
enjoy sensual pleasures and take your delight in them;
having abandoned the army of Pañcāla,”
“Brahmadatta is fleeing.
“The king, desiring intimacy with you,
offers you his treasures.”
Let messengers come from here,
sweet-voiced and pleasant-spoken;
let them speak words that are gentle.
Whatever words have been spoken in response,
may both Pañcāla and Videha become one for you.
“Tell me now, Keṭubha, how was the meeting with Mahosadha? Pray, tell me this:
was he appeased by you?”
“Is Mahosadha content?
“He is a man of ignoble character, O Lord of Men;
he does not greet others, he is stubborn, and he is ungentlemanly.”
"Just as one who is mute and deaf would not speak anything at all, so too [is this verse].
Truly, this line of the mantra is very difficult to see."
The goal has been seen as pure through human effort;
for thus my body trembles—
having abandoned it myself, who would send it into another's hands?
For the wise who have attained the highest and most abundant success, there is but one single resolve that accords with them:
whether it be a vehicle, a non-vehicle, or even a state of standing still.
“Mahosadha, you too must apply your intelligence.
“You know well, O King, that the powerful Brahmadatta of Cūḷani is of great majesty and great strength.”
And the king desires his death,
just as a hunter seeks a deer in its own haunts;
he is like a fish caught on a hook.
The hook is concealed by meat;
greedy for the raw flesh, the fish does not know its own death.
In just this way, O King,
you, greedy for sensual pleasures, do not recognize the daughter of Cūḷaneyya.
Like a fish to its own death.
If you go to Pañcāla,
you will quickly cast off your life.
“Like a deer following a path,
great danger will come upon you.
“We alone are fools and dull-witted,” [they said].
"We have spoken to you of the highest goals;
why is it that you, like one grown at the tip of a plowshare, do not understand these matters as others do?"
“Seize him by the throat and destroy him, O conquerors of mine!
He who [thwarts] my acquisition of the jewels— ”
He speaks for the sake of creating obstacles.
Then, having departed from the presence of the King of Videha, he...
Then he addressed the messenger Mādhara, who was very wise:
"Come, friend Haritapakkha!"
"Perform service for me;
the King of Pañcāla has a female parrot who guards his bed."
Ask her about that bond,
for she is skilled in all things;
she knows everything concerning them.
“Of the king and of Kosiya.
Having replied, “Yes,” Mādhara, the very wise one, [acted accordingly].
The green-winged parrot arrived at the presence of the sāḷikā; and then,
having gone there, he—
Then the very wise Madhava consulted his dear wife,
the sweet-voiced sāḷikā bird.
“I hope all is well in your fine home, O Vessa; I hope you are free from illness.
I hope you have honeyed parched grain.”
“May you find a good home.
“I am indeed well, my friend,
and moreover, I am free from illness;”
"Furthermore, O very wise one,
parched grain with honey is obtained by me.
From where indeed, good sir, have you come?"
"By whom have you been sent?
For you have never been seen or heard of by us before."
“I was the bed-keeper in the palace of King Sivi;
then that righteous king— ”
When I was bound, you released me from my bonds.
You were his one companion,
that sweet-voiced sāḷika bird.
There, while I was looking on from my fine house, the army destroyed him;
for he was indeed devoted to sensual pleasures.
I have come into your presence;
if you would grant me the opportunity,
let us both dwell together.
“A male sunbird might desire a female sunbird,
and a male sālika bird a female sālika bird;
but for the sunbird, it is only the female sālika.”
“What kind of cohabitation is there?
“Whoever desires sensual pleasures—
even those of a Caṇḍāla woman— ”
"For everyone is alike; there is no one among those who desire that is not like them.
"There is one named Jampāvatī..."
She was the mother of King Sivi;
she was the wife of Vāsudeva,
the beloved chief queen of Kaṇha.
The Kimpurisa woman Raṭṭhavatī also desired Vaccha;
so too did the human man with the female deer.
There is nothing among desires that is its equal.
Come now, I shall go,
O Sāḷikā of sweet voice!
“This is indeed the consequence of rejection;
surely you despise me.
“Fortune does not belong to one who is in haste;”
O Mādhara, you who are very wise:
stay right here for now until you see the king.
"Such is the sound of the drums,
and such is the majesty of the king.
"This intense sound that has arisen..."
A son born in another kingdom,
a daughter of the King of Pañcāla,
radiant in complexion like a medicinal herb.
"He will give her to the Videhans;
that shall be the wedding.
"O enemies, let it not be so!"
Let there be a marriage,
not an inferior one; let it be between the King of Pañcāla and the Prince of Videha.
Having brought the Vedeḥan princess,
the bull among charioteers of the Pañcālas will then have her executed.
“...she will become my friend.
“Well then, grant me leave for seven nights;”
I shall inform King Śivi that I have found a dwelling place for the Great Sage.
"To the presence of the sāḷikā.
"Very well then, I grant you that for seven nights."
If you do not come into my presence within seven nights,
I think that my life-force has already departed.
"You will come when she has died.
Then Mādhara, the very wise one, having gone there, [said]:
She related these words of the sāḷika bird to Mahosadha:
“In whosevery house one should eat, that wealth— ”
A man should live according to that very purpose;
come now, O Lord of Men, I shall go to the most delightful city of the King of Pañcāla.
To have dwellings built for the illustrious Vedeha; having had the dwellings built, [he gave them].
Of the illustrious King of Videha; when I send for you,
then you should come, O Kshatriya.”
Then Mahosadha departed from the city toward the most delightful city of the King of Pañcāla,
in order to have dwellings constructed.
Having built dwellings for the illustrious Vedeha,
for the illustrious Vedeha.
Then he dispatched a messenger to Vedeha,
the ruler of Mithilā:
“Come now, O Great King!”
"Your dwelling has been built.
Then King Pāyāsi set out with his fourfold army.
Having seen Anantavāhana and the prosperous city of Kapilavatthu,
he then departed from there.
She sent word to Brahmadatta:
"I have come, O Great King,
to pay homage at your feet."
Now give me a wife,
a woman beautiful in every limb, adorned with gold.
“Accompanied by a host of female slaves.
“Welcome to you, O Vedeha;
indeed, you have come from afar.”
Ask about the very constellations,
maiden; I shall give you a [gift] covered with gold.
“Honored by a host of female slaves.
Then King Videha inquired about the auspicious conjunction of the stars.
Having inquired about the auspicious constellations,
he sent word to Brahmadatta:
"Now give me your wife."
A woman beautiful in every limb,
adorned with gold, and attended by a retinue of female servants.
“I now give you this wife,
a woman beautiful in every limb,
covered with gold.”
"Accompanied by a retinue of female slaves.
"Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—
the army stands arrayed in full armor."
Torches are burning and glowing;
what do the wise think of this?
Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—
The army stands armored,
torches are burning and glowing;
what indeed will they do against a wise man?
“O Great King, the mighty Cūḷaneyya protects him;
he has been provoked by Brahmadatta.”
“At dawn he will cause him to be killed.
“My heart trembles and my mouth dries up;”
I do not attain peace,
like one scorched by fire in the heat;
I am like the torch of smiths.
It meditates within, not without;
even so my heart meditates within, not without.
“Negligent and having transgressed the counsel,
you have broken the counsel, O Kṣatriya;
may they now protect you!”
Wise people who possess counsel,
though desiring his welfare and seeking his benefit, do not carry out the words of a minister who acts against his own interest.
The king, delighting in self-pleasure,
is like a deer caught in a trap,
or like a fish on a hook.
The hook is concealed by meat;
greedy for the raw flesh, the fish does not know its own death.
In the same way, O King, you,
greedy for sensual pleasures, do not realize that this is the daughter of Cūḷaneyya.
Like a fish [longing for water],
you will abandon your life if you go to Pañcāla;
you will quickly cast it away.
Like a deer following a path,
great danger will come upon you,
O Lord of Men, for that man is of ignoble character.
Like a snake that has crept into one's lap,
a wise person should not form friendship with such a one;
for association with a base man is indeed painful.
O Lord of Men, when one knows a person to be virtuous and learned,
a wise man should form friendship with that very person.
Happy indeed is the meeting with a true person.
But you are a fool and a mute, O King,
you who prattle away at the highest goals to me.
"Why should I not understand matters as others do, like one who has grown up at the tip of a plough?
Having seized him by the throat,"
"Destroy those who have conquered me;
whoever speaks for the sake of creating an obstacle to my acquisition of the jewels."
“O Mahosadha, the wise do not pierce with the past:
‘Why am I bound like a horse?’”
You strike with a goad alone.
If you see liberation,
or if you see safety;
“Instruct me by that alone;
why do you strike with the past?
“Human action of the past—”
It is difficult to do, hard to achieve;
I am not able to release him—
understand this, O Khattiya.
There are indeed nāgas who move through the air,
possessing supernormal powers and great renown;
they too might come taking [him] with them.
For whom there exist such as these: steeds capable of traveling through the air,
possessed of supernormal power and great renown.
Those who possess such wings as these may take flight and go through the air;
yet there are birds that fly through the sky.
Possessing supernormal powers and renowned fame—
those for whom such as these exist may take them along and go.
There are indeed yakkhas in the air,
possessing psychic power and renown;
they too might take him and go away.
For whomsoever such [qualities] exist:
human deeds of the past that were difficult to perform and hard to accomplish.
“I am not able to release him,
O Kṣatriya, even by way of the air.
“A man who does not see the further shore...”
In a vast expanse of water,
wherever he finds a firm footing,
there he finds happiness.
Thus, for both me and the king,
you are our support, Mahosadha;
you are the best among those possessed of wisdom.
“Deliver us from suffering!
“Human karma of the past is difficult to perform and difficult to accomplish.”
“I am not able to release him;
you yourself must understand this, Senaka.
“Listen to these words of mine:”
Behold this great danger!
Now I ask Senaka:
what do you consider should be done here?
“Either we shall give the fire from the doorway,
or we shall take up the carving-knife;
having slain one another, [we shall depart].”
We shall quickly give up our lives,
lest King Brahmadatta kill us with prolonged suffering.”
“Listen to these words of mine;
behold this army, a source of great terror!
Now I ask you, Pukkusa:”
"What do you think should be done here?
"We shall die having swallowed poison;
we will quickly end our lives."
“May King Brahmadatta not cause us to die for long in suffering.
“Listen to these words of mine:”
Behold this army of great terror!
Now I ask the Lord of Desire:
what do you consider should be done here?
“We are being bound with ropes;
we are falling down precipices.
May King Brahmadatta not [seize] us!”
“Kill me with long-lasting suffering.
“Listen to these words of mine:
behold this army, a source of great terror!”
"Now I ask you, O Lord of Devas:
what do you think should be done here?
"We shall give fire from the gateway," he replied.
We shall seize the instrument of dismemberment;
having struck one another down,
we shall swiftly end our lives.
“Mahosadha cannot release us with ease.
“As if seeking the core of a plantain tree,”
Though we searched, we did not find it;
thus, though searching for him,
we have not attained the answer to our question.
Just as one seeking the core of a śimbalī tree does not find it,
so too, while searching for it, [one finds nothing].
We could not find an answer.
Truly, it rained upon us in the wrong place—
upon the elephants in the forest water.
In the presence of those base men,
fools who lack understanding,
my heart trembles.
And my mouth dries up;
I find no peace,
like one scorched by fire in the heat of the sun.
Just as the forge-fire of smiths glows within but not without,
even so is my heart.
“He meditates within, not without.
Then that wise and steadfast one,
the seer of truth, Mahosadha—
Seeing Vedeha afflicted with pain,
he spoke these words:
“Do not fear, O Great King.”
Do not fear, O bull among chariot-warriors;
I shall release you,
as Rāhu releases the moon.
Do not fear, O Great King;
do not fear, O Bull among Charioteers;
I shall set you free.
Like the sun seized by the planet Rāhu.
Do not fear, O Great King;
do not fear, O Bull among Charioteers.
I shall deliver you,
like an elephant sunk in the mud.
Do not fear, O Great King!
Do not fear, O bull among charioteers;
I shall release you,
like a serpent confined within a basket.
Do not fear, O Great King;
do not fear, O Bull among Charioteers.
I shall set you free.
Like a bird bound in a cage.
Do not fear, O Great King;
do not fear, O Bull among Charioteers!
I shall release you,
like a fish caught in a net;
do not fear, O Great King.
Do not fear, O bull among chariot-warriors;
I shall deliver you, along with your horses, troops, and vehicles.
Do not fear, O Great King;
do not fear, O Bull among Charioteers;
I shall drive you to Pañcāla.
Like a clod of earth against a crow—
what is the use of wisdom,
or even such a counselor?
“He who does not liberate one who has fallen into that strait from suffering.
“Come, young men, arise!”
“Cleanse the passes and the fortifications;
Vedeha, together with his ministers,
will come by way of Umaṅga.”
Having heard those words of his,
the attendants of the wise man opened the gate of Umanga.
And when the bolts were fitted,
Senaka went in front and Mahosadha followed behind.
And in the middle was King Vedeha,
surrounded by his ministers;
having departed from Umanga, he—
Videha boarded the boat;
and knowing that he had embarked,
Mahosadha instructed him.
“This is your father-in-law, O King,
and this is your mother-in-law, O Lord of Men; the manner of conduct toward them is the same as that toward one’s own mother.”
May it be so with your mother-in-law,
just as with a brother who is one's own kinsman,
born of the same womb and from the same mother.
Thus, O Bull among Charioteers, this Pañcālacandī must be given to you.
This Pañcālacandī is yours.
"The princess is desired by you;
do as you wish with her,
O bull among chariot-warriors— she shall be your wife."
“Having boarded the boat and hastening across,
why indeed do you stand on the shore?
We have been released from suffering with great difficulty.”
“Let us go now, Mahosadha.
“This is not the way, Great King,
for me who am the leader of the army.”
Having abandoned the army,
O King, you should liberate yourself from this dwelling.
That army unit has been lost; O bull among charioteers,
it was given away by Brahmadatta,
and I shall bring it back.”
“How will you, with a small army,
stand in opposition to a great army?
How can the weak contend with the powerful?”
“You will be frustrated, O wise one.
“Even if a counselor with a small army advises against a king with a great army who does not listen,”
“A king overcomes other kings,
just as the rising sun overcomes darkness.
How truly happy is the life together!”
"By the wise," O Senaka,
"like birds bound in a cage,
or like fish caught in a net."
“Mahosadha rescued us when we had fallen into the hands of our enemies.
“It is even so, Great King.”
For the wise bring happiness,
like a bird released from a cage,
or a fish from the net.
When he had fallen into the hands of his enemies,
Mahosadha did not release him;
having guarded him throughout the entire night, [he brought him back].”
Cūḷaneyya, possessed of great strength,
approached his benefactor as the dawn was rising.
Having mounted his excellent elephant,
powerful and sixty years of age,
the King of Pañcāla spoke:
Cūḷaneyya, possessed of great strength,
was armored with a jewel-encrusted coat of mail and took up an arrow in his hand.
Pesiya addressed those who had gathered in various groups—
elephant riders and those stationed in the army ranks.
Charioteers, infantrymen,
those skilled in the art of attendance,
and fletchers have arrived.
“Drive forth the tusker elephants,
powerful and sixty years of age;
let the elephants trample the city.”
It was well-fashioned by the King of Videha.
With ivory tips that are white,
sharp-pointed, and capable of piercing bone;
Driven by the force of the bow,
the brave young archers rushed at one another.
Let the great warriors, armed with variegated spears and leaping into battle,
stand face-to-face against the elephants.
Let the spears, washed with oil,
blazing and radiant,
stand shining forth.
Like a four-rayed star,
[he shines] among those powerful in weaponry who wear bracelets and armlets.
How can Vedeha escape from such warriors who do not flee in battle?
If he should act like a bird:
my thirty-nine men, all of them individually determined.
I see no one equal to them as they wander through the entire world—
these well-trained, tamed elephants.
Strong and sixty years of age,
yet upon their shoulders shine youths of lovely appearance.
Adorned with yellow ornaments, clad in yellow garments,
and wearing yellow upper robes,
they shine upon the trunks of the nāgas.
Like young gods in the Nandana grove,
they were the color of pāṭhīna fish, with prominent eyes,
shining bright as if washed with oil.
These well-composed and firmly grounded verses,
free from stains and devoid of impurity,
have been completed by those wise among men.
The straps of leather were firm,
held by strong men capable of delivering powerful blows.
Endowed with golden stalks and bearing crimson petals,
they shine as they unfurl.
Like lightning amidst thick clouds.
Warriors wearing turbans and carrying banners,
skilled in the use of sword and shield;
Surrounded by such archers,
highly trained and capable of striking down the bodies of elephants—
"There is no escape for you from this;
I see no power by which you might go to Mithilā."
"Why indeed did you send forth the elephant, that great tusker, in such haste?
You have arrived here with a joyful countenance."
"You think, 'I am Siddhattha.
Take away this bow and arrow;
withdraw your sharp shaft."
“Your beautiful armor, inlaid with beryl and jewels,
has been stripped away. “You have the complexion of one whose face is serene.”
And you speak with moderation;
such is the perfection of complexion one possesses at the time of death.
“Vain was your thundering, O King;
you are one whose counsel has been broken, O Kshatriya.
It will be difficult for you to seize the king.”
Like thoroughbred steeds with their colts,
the king crossed the Ganges yesterday together with his ministers and his retinue.
Like a vulture against a king of swans,
you will fly contrary to the current; like jackals during the night-time portion.
Seeing a blossoming *kiṃsuka* tree,
those base deer, thinking it was a piece of meat, rushed toward it.
When the nights had passed away and the sun had risen,
having seen the *kiṃsuka* tree in full bloom, [he thought:]...
Like a deer caught in a snare,
even so you, O King,
have surrounded the Prince of Videha.
"You will go with your neck severed,
like a jackal to a *kiṃsuka* tree.
"In this man's hands and feet..."
Cut off his ears and nose,
he who has liberated from my hands my enemy,
the Prince of Videha.
"This flesh must be eaten; having impaled him on a stake, let them cook him—
whoever has my enemy fallen into his hands."
He liberated Vedeha.
Just as a bull's hide is stretched out upon the earth, so too was he spread abroad.
For the lion and for the tiger,
there is a well-strung bowstring;
having thus stretched it out, [one should...]
I shall pierce him with my spear—
he who liberated from my hand my enemy, the Videhan.”
“If you cut off my hands and feet,
and my ears and nose,
even so, O Pañcālacanda— ”
The King of Videha will cause them to be cut off.
If you were to cut off my hands and feet,
as well as my ears and nose;
In this way, Vedeha will cause the hands and feet of Pañcālacandī to be cut off, if they are in my hands.
"You shall have your ears and nose cut off;
thus will the King of Videha cause Queen Nandā to be mutilated."
If you should cut off my hands and feet,
and my ears and nose,
thus [it will be] for your wife and children.
The King of Videha will have me cut up.
If my flesh must be eaten,
you shall roast it after impaling it on a spit.
In this way, Vedeha will cause Pañcālacanda to be cooked;
if indeed flesh were to be drunk, [it would be so].
Having impaled him on a stake,
you shall cook him; thus will the King of Videha cause the Queen of Pañcāla to be cooked.
If meat were to be drunk,
you would roast it after skewering it on a spit;
such is the case for Queen Nandā.
The King of Videha will cook it.
If meat must indeed be cooked,
you shall cook it after skewering it on a spit.
In this way, Vedeha will cause suffering for you and your wife and children,
even if he were to stretch out his arms toward me.
"You shall pierce him with a spear;
thus will the King of Videha pierce the Moon of Pañcāla."
If, having drawn back [your bow],
you would strike me with a spear,
even so, O Pañcālacandī—
Vedeha will strike you back.
If, having drawn your bow,
you strike me with a spear;
In this way, Vedeha will pierce Queen Nandā;
even if he were to stretch me out,
[he would not reach her].
"You shall pierce him with a spear;
thus shall Vedeha pierce you, along with your wife and children."
Thus was it deliberated by us in secret,
by me together with the Vedehe,
just like a hide weighing a hundred palas.
The final meditation has been completed;
it serves to thin out the afflictions in order to ward off the arrows of passion.
Bringing happiness and dispelling suffering for the illustrious Vedeha,
I shall counteract your intellect.
Or even with a hundred thousand spears.
Come now, look, Great King:
your inner palace is empty.
The Orodhas and the Kumāras,
and your mother, O Kṣatriya— having brought them out from Umanga, [they were placed] there.
“Come now, having gone to my inner palace, search for her.”
“Whether his word be true or false.
“It is even so, Great King.”
As Mahosadha said:
"The entire inner palace is empty,
like a village of crows."
“Here has come, O Great King,
a woman beautiful in all her limbs,
with hips as lovely as the wood-apple fruit.”
"O Great King, this woman, beautiful in every limb and speaking with a voice like a swan's cry, has been led away from here."
Clad in silk garments,
with a beautiful girdle of gold,
she was lovely, with feet of a beautiful red hue.
With a girdle of gold and jewels,
with eyes like the pārevata bird, she was slender-limbed,
with lips like the bimba fruit and a delicate waist.
Sujātā has arms like slender creepers,
a waist as slim as an altar,
and long, black hair.
Slightly flickering at the tip,
like well-crafted deer-horns,
or like the crest of a winter fire.
Like a river in mountain fastnesses,
overgrown with small reeds,
she who is beautiful as the trunk of an elephant— Kalyāṇī.
She has thighs like the finest *timbaru* fruit;
she is neither too tall nor too short,
neither hairless nor excessively hairy.
“Surely you rejoice at Nandā’s death, O Sirivāhana;
surely both I and Nandā— ”
"Let us go to Yama's abode.
"You practice celestial illusion and have created this delusion of the eye."
“He who liberated from my hand my enemy,
the prince of Videha. “They are studying,
O Great King,” [he replied].
The wise here dispel celestial illusion;
those wise people, possessed of discernment, liberate themselves.
I have young men who are skilled at cutting joints,
by whose made path—
“Videha has gone to Mithilā.
“Come now, Great King,
behold the well-constructed Umanga;”
Of elephants, horses,
chariots, and infantry—
standing as a source of light.
“The city’s moat has been well constructed.
“It is indeed a gain for the Videhans that such wise men as these dwell among them.”
“Dwelling at home within your own domain, just as you are, O Mahosadha. [He replied:
“Both my livelihood and my protection—”
I give you double the food and wages; enjoy vast riches,
partake of sensual pleasures, and take your delight in them.
"Do not go to Videha; what will Videha do for you?
"O Great King, he who would renounce..."
For the sake of wealth,
one who abandons his master is censurable both by himself and by others.
"As long as Vedeha lives,
O Great King, he shall not become the servant of another who would abandon [him]."
For the sake of wealth,
one who abandons his master is blameworthy for both himself and for the other.
“As long as Vedeha remains,
he shall not live under the sway of another’s kingdom.
“I give you a thousand pieces of gold;”
In Kāsi, I gave you eight hundred cows;
I give you four hundred female slaves and a hundred wives.
Taking all your troops with you,
Mahosadha, go in safety until they give [the elephants] to us.
Let them provide double the rations for the horses;
let them satisfy with food and drink the charioteers and the infantrymen.
Let the wise man go taking with him elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry;
let the Great King see him.
“The King of Videha has gone to Mithilā.
“Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—
the great army is visible.”
“An army of four divisions, terrifying in appearance—
what do you think of this, O wise one?
“It would be a source of joy for you, Great King.”
The supreme one was seen;
having taken his entire army,
Mahosadha reached safety.
"Just as these four people have abandoned this [body] at the cemetery,
so too, O Kapilayī, have we."
Having abandoned [them], you have come here.
Now, for what reason, or by what cause, [have you done so]?
“By what kind of matter did he liberate himself? “O Videha,
by means of one thing through another thing,” [he replied].
With counsel, O Kshatriya,
I surrounded the king,
just as the ocean surrounds Jambudvīpa.
“A thousand gold coins were given to me,
and eighty villages in Kāsi;
four hundred female slaves— ”
"A hundred wives were given to me;
taking my entire army with me,
I have returned here in safety."
“Truly happy is the dwelling with the wise,” said Senaka,
“like birds confined within a cage.”
Like fish that have entered a net,
Mahosadha could not release those who had fallen into the hands of their enemies.
“So it is, great king;
for the wise bring happiness,
like birds bound within a cage.”
Like fish caught in a net,
Mahosadha could not release those who had fallen into the hands of their enemies.
“Let all lutes be struck,
and the kettledrums and small drums;
let the Magadhan conchs be blown.”
“Let the drums resound joyfully!”—
the courtiers and princes,
the merchants and brahmins;
They brought much food and drink for the wise man;
elephant-riders and those stationed in the ranks, too.
Charioteers and infantrymen brought much food and drink for the wise man.
The people of the countryside have gathered,
and the townspeople have gathered;
there is much food and drink.
The multitude was filled with faith upon seeing the arrival of the wise man. "You are well-pleased," they said,
"having seen the wise one come."
"When the wise man arrived,
the tossing of the garment ceased.
Thus ends the *Umaṅga Jātaka*, the fifth.
